sentences.text: Huinculsaurus is known from a single species, Huinculsaurus montesi, based on five partial vertebrae that were not fully fused, leading researchers to believe the holotype was an immature individual.
Based on these remains, scientists estimate that the animal was around 3.42 meters long in life.
This dinosaur is distinguished from other theropods by unique vertebral features such as elongated articular facets, pneumatic foramina, and an accessory lamina.
The species name montesi honors Eduardo Montes, a fossil preparator who died shortly before the official publication of the species.
The vertebrae of Huinculsaurus were mechanically separated during preparation before the genus was formally published in 2020.
The fossils of Huinculsaurus were discovered around 1991 in the Huincul Formation in Neuquén, Argentina, near the site of the Ilokelesia holotype.
Researchers suggest Huinculsaurus may have occupied a different ecological niche, possibly as an omnivore or herbivore with a cursorial lifestyle, due to its coexistence with large predators.
Huinculsaurus coexisted with the abelisaurid Ilokelesia at the same locality.
The Huincul Formation contains fossils of titanosaurs like Argentinosaurus and rebbachisaurids like Cathartesaura.
Phylogenetic analyses suggest Huinculsaurus is a close relative of the Late Jurassic theropod Elaphrosaurus.
The precise classification of Huinculsaurus is difficult because its vertebrae share similarities with both Noasauridae and Abelisauridae.
Despite these similarities, Huinculsaurus is classified within the family Noasauridae and assigned to the subfamily Elaphrosaurinae.
The subfamily Elaphrosaurinae includes graceful theropods of small to medium size, such as Elaphrosaurus and Limusaurus.
Huinculsaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Albian stage.
The fossil record for Huinculsaurus spans from 110.1 to 106.3 million years ago.
Huinculsaurus is the latest known member of the Elaphrosaurinae subfamily.
The Huincul Formation, where Huinculsaurus was found, consists of yellowish and greenish fine-to-medium grain sandstones, some containing volcanic ash.
The environment of the Huincul Formation is thought to have been arid with ephemeral or seasonal streams.
Fossilized pollen from the Huincul Formation indicates the presence of hornworts, liverworts, ferns, conifers, and some flowering plants.
Hypotheses regarding the evolutionary relationships of Huinculsaurus are considered preliminary due to a lack of small ceratosaur fossils.
